newsitem.title: THAILAND: Unemployment rears head in crisis-hit Thailand.
newsitem.headline: Unemployment rears head in crisis-hit Thailand.

text.p: Broker Suvapee's dreams of going on a long vacation abroad were near impossible in the past when Thailand's booming financial markets kept her and her finance and securities company very busy.
But now her dreams have come true, in a paradoxical way, as the Thai financial market and economy goes from boom to bust.
She can go on long holidays every other month, if she wants to, with her company's blessings...but without pay.
Suvapee's (not her real name) is one of many in Thailand whose jobs have been hit as a result of the nation's crisis-hit and sharply slowing economy.

In fact, she's better off than many of her peers who are being laid off outright, especially by depressed finance and securities firms, desperate to cut costs as the downturn and a lingering financial crisis bites into their bottom lines.

Thailand's once robust economy posted average nine percent growth annually for a decade until it ran into trouble last year. Private economists see Thai 1997 growth plummeting to between three and five percent this year from 6.4 percent in 1996,
Things were going so well for the country in the past that unemployment was never a problem and the Bank of Thailand did not report jobs data as part of leading monthly economic indicators.
During the boom, all those in the bubbly finance sector were concerned about was whether their bonuses would be higher than the equivalent of six-months salary, which was the norm.
But unemployment is now starting to rear its ugly head and several firms have begun downsizing their workforces since late last year, industry experts said.

Although the magnitude of joblessness is not as bad as in some other countries, analysts see it escalating in the near future as a looming massive shake-up of the troubled finance sector is likely to see more mergers or collapses of finance firms.
Thailand's finance companies plunged deep into trouble because of soaring non-performing loans caused by billions of dollars in exposure to the beleaguered property sector.

A glut and sharp decline in property prices have eroded the asset quality and collateral values of loans from financial institutions. Current high interest rates have choked businesses, exports have turned sluggish, the stock market is at an eight-year-low and speculators have attacked the embattled baht.

Supavud Saicheau, chief economist at Phatra Thanakit Plc, believes half of the 30,000-50,000 employees in the finance and securities sector could loose their jobs as the industry enters a period of much-needed consolidation.

"There are 91 finance firms now...It is inevitable that they have to consolidate to survive. Half of the work force will either relocate to other sectors or become unemployed," he said. "How fast these excess will be absorbed depend on how fast the economy turns around."

The Bank of Thailand, in an attempt to avert financial melt-down, is pressing the troubled sector to consolidate. But despite trying to use a carrot and stick approach little has materialised so far that the central bank can be proud of.

Last month's collapse of a so-called mega-merger between Thailand's largest finance company Finance One and medium-sized Thai Danu Bank, billed as a trailblazer for the rest of the sector, sent shockwaves through the industry.
The authorities, undaunted by the failure, have again pledged to come up with newer guidelines to make mergers easier which analysts say will not bode well for employment in the sector.

The pain of joblessness is not limited to the finance sector alone and is spreading quickly. Almost 10,000 people in Thailand's less competitive labour-intensive industries such as textile and footwear have been laid off as factories move to lower costs.
In the service sector, hotels, advertising and travel firms are feeling the pinch and say jobs are not safe.

"And you will see more of that in the future. We are dealing with both cyclical and structural problems here. First, factories are cutting costs as exports plummeted and downsizing the workforce is one of the most viable options," said Saengchai Ekpatpanich, a member of the powerful Federation of Thai Industries.

"Second, there is also a need to restructure in order to be competitive in the future. Many import new machinery to upgrade the products...and that will partly replace some human work forces. Those with skill with survive," he said.
